newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH CROWN FLOAT NEEDS WAGE RISE CHECKS - ANALYSTS.
newsitem.headline: CZECH CROWN FLOAT NEEDS WAGE RISE CHECKS - ANALYSTS.

text.p: The Czech National Bank's (CNB) decision to allow the crown to float will cut economic growth and boost inflation this year and must be reinforced by strict control of wage increases, economists said on Tuesday.
The CNB said late on Monday it was abolishing the bands within which the crown moves against a mark/dollar basket, calling the new regime a "controlled float".
It raised its key discount rate to 13 percent from 10.5 percent, indicating it would keep monetary policy tight.

"If they are not able to have fiscal and monetary restrictions, there will be inflation, wage growth, loss of competitiveness and further devaluation, a vicious circle," said economist Vladimir Kreidl of Patria Finance.

"I hope that we will be able to cut expenditure to keep wages under control, and money supply, which would imply higher interest rates. If they are able to do that...we will se no economic growth this year," he added.
Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, sitting alongside central bank governor Josef Tosovsky, told a news conference on Monday that the government would not abandon fiscal or monetary stability.
Klaus said the government was prepared for further spending cuts to keep the budget in balance and would seek an agreement with workers and employers to prevent a wage spiral.
"Until there is a new equilibrium of the exchange rate, interest rates will probably be maintained at this relatively high level," said analyst Jiri Krovak of Wood & Company.

"Some economic activity will slow and some will stop so the overall effect on economic growth will be negative," he said, adding the depth of the slowdown would depend on how long it took for the crown to stabilise. The "upper limit" for GDP growth this year would be two percent.
The crown has been under severe selling pressure for the past 10 days as investors, alarmed at wideing trade and current account deficits and a fall in output, drove the crown down.

The government unveiled a package of measures last month intended to restore balance to the economy, including 25.5 billion crowns in spending cuts and a 7.3 percent limit on public sector wage growth, down from a budgeted 11.9 percent.
"The most important task of the government is not to allow wages to reflect the depreciation of the currency," said Zivnostenska banka chief economist Pavel Sobisek.
The Czech Statistical Bureau this month revised its forecasts, saying GDP would grow between 2.9 and 3.5 percent this year and that average inflation would be 8.2-8.8 percent.

"This new level of the currency will definitely restrict some activity and decrease domestic demand which will reflect negatively on GDP," said Sobisek, adding GDP would grow between zero and two percent this year.
Krovak said strong competition on the domestic retail market would prevent importers from passing on the full effect of the weaker crown on import prices.

"Our prediction is that if we forecast a 10 percent weakening of the crown it will increase domestic inflation by 1.5 percent," he said, adding this would raise his forecast to 9.5 percent for the year.
Sobisek said a crown depreciation of 10 percent against its old basket parity would dramatically improve Czech export competitiveness and that imports would decline.
Kreidl, however, said the stimulus of exports would only be felt after several months. Annual inflation this year could exceed 10 percent, instead of an earlier forecast 8.5 percent.
